rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands clean: it turns the same facts into usable labor, consumer, operations, and IPO angles while repeatedly naming the holes it cannot fill. A's strongest line is the proof caveat under "Klarna's AI now does the work of 700 agents — and its headcount fell 20%": "this gap must be acknowledged in any pitch." B has good bones, but "Klarna won't say how many of the jobs it cut were actually replaced by AI" commits the exact sin the facts warn against: making causality sound cleaner than it is.
gaps_in_A: "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" overstates the supplied facts. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes; it does not say the chatbot decides disputes.
"The headcount number and the IPO filing make this a live" leans on IPO status as timeliness without a dated filing event. A catches this later, but the peg is still warm, not hot.
"Klarna cut average chat resolution from 11 minutes to under 2 — here's how" is a trade deep-dive, not much of a news angle unless Klarna provides real operational detail beyond its own speed stat.
gaps_in_B: "Klarna won't say how many of the jobs it cut were actually replaced by AI" invents too much. The facts say headcount fell, hiring froze, and Klarna will not separate cuts from unfilled roles; they do not prove AI replacement.
"Klarna's AI is now handling disputes" is not established. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that Klarna confirmed AI handles or decides them.

"The most-mocked category of enterprise AI might actually be working" imports a whole zeitgeist the update did not supply, then softens it with "if Klarna's numbers hold up." That's clever padding, not grounding.
"Decay: 24hr" and "The IPO filing is the live event" manufacture urgency. The facts say Klarna has filed to go public, but provide no date, prospectus detail, or same-day trigger.
